chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, and Muhammad ibn Ismail, from Al-Fadl ibn Shazan, all from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Umar ibn Udhaynah, from Zurara, who said:

I was sitting beside Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), and he was sitting with his arms around his knees, facing the Ka'bah. He said: 'Indeed, looking at it is an act of worship.' Then a man from Bajilah came to him, called Asim ibn Umar, and said to Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him): 'Ka'b al-Ahbar used to say that the Ka'bah prostrates to Bayt al-Maqdis every morning.' Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said: 'So what do you say about what Ka'b said?' He said: 'He spoke the truth; the statement is what Ka'b said.' Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said: 'You lied, and Ka'b al-Ahbar lied with you,' and he was angered.

Zurara said: 'I did not see him face anyone else by saying 'You lied' except him.' Then he said: 'Allah, Mighty and Majestic, did not create a spot on the earth more beloved to Him than it.' Then he gestured with his hand towards the Ka'bah, and said: 'Nor is anything more prestigious to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, than it. For it, Allah sanctified the sacred months in His Book the day He created the heavens and the earth: three consecutive ones for the Hajj — Shawwal, Dhu al-Qadah, and Dhu al-Hijjah — and a separate month for the Umrah, which is Rajab.'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on looking at the Ka'bah and what is its status in Islam?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) refutes the anthropomorphic view of Ka'bah prostrating to Jerusalem, affirming its unique status as the most beloved spot on earth to Allah. The narration further elucidates the divine institution of the four sacred months, distinguishing the three consecutive months for Hajj from the solitary month of Rajab designated for Umrah.
